newsitem.title: UK: British utilities square up to windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: British utilities square up to windfall tax.

text.p: Britain's water and electricity firms, which are potentially facing a one-off tax on so-called excess profits by the new Labour government, have begun to start lobbying as their annual results trickle in.

Paymaster General Geoffrey Robinson, who is responsible for implementing the levy, has asked firms to submit comments by the end of May. Regulators will give their views on the proposed tax over the next two weeks.
A Finance Ministry spokesman said around a dozen companies had been in to see officials so far while there had also been "a number of written submissions."
"It's a fair spread (from) anyone who feels they may be drawn into the windfall net," the official said.

The one-off tax, aimed at funding a 3.0 billion pound ($4.9 billion) programme to cut unemployment and fund training, is a central plank of policy for the new Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1.
The government has refused to be drawn on details of the tax such as total amount to be raised or which companies will be affected.
Details are being closely guarded until its first budget, the date of which will be announced on Monday.

"There is going to be a tax. We are not willing to take (consider) arguments about that," the treasury spokesman said. But he added that submissions would be considered over technical aspects of the levy.
A tax of around five billion pounds has largely been factored in by the market across a range of possible targets, analysts say.
British Telecommunication Plc's chairman Sir Iain Vallance kicked off threats mid-month when he said he would challenge the tax "if we are stung in a big way and if it can be challenged legally."

But electricity and water companies, thought to be prime targets for the tax after heavy criticism from Labour over their bumper profits, dividends and executive pay packets, seem largely resigned to some form of levy.
As their annual results trickle in, the companies have tackled the issue from each individual's standpoint, rather than attempting a broad-based argument against the tax.

Last week, electricity generating giant National Power, said it had made no excess profits, argued taxpayers had already benefitted because it was sold in tranches, allowing the state to reap the benefit of share price rises and dividends in between sales.

PowerGen, the second generator sold off at the same time as National Power, declined to comment on the tax when releasing results on Thursday, but newspaper reports suggested it might adopt a similar argument.
This week, it was the turn of the water companies to weigh in as they all posted higher profits, with Anglian Water first to comment at its results on Tuesday.
The company said it felt the tax was unfair but that if it were levied, proceeds should be "fed back into the Anglian region".
"That could be good for company images, using the proceeds to help local people," one analyst said.
"Which of these arguments will be taken into account is anybody's guess. But it all becomes more of an issue if the tax is huge," he added.
On Thursday, multi-utility United Utilities said it hoped the government would treat it leniently over the tax because it had already shared benefits with all stakeholders including customers.
South West Water, which also reported annual results on Thursday, declined to comment on the tax until it has seen details.
Yorkshire Water on Friday admitted it had assumed a windfall levy in financial calculations -- although it declined to give a figure.
Chairman Brandon Gough said: "The issue is on what basis will it be levied as much as how much it will be."
Analysts suggest that the government might give a broad framework for the levy but then pinpoint a tighter range of companies through methods used to assess excess profits.
"The windfall tax needs a broad base otherwise it will be open to claims of discrimination and possible legal challenges," said one analyst.
